--- title: "Pandas Tutorial: Selecting, Reading, and Combining Data" error: true --- ## Goals 1. Select rows and columns by **label** (`.loc`) and by **position** (`.iloc`). 2. Control how files are read and written, and combine several files into one table. 3. Combine tables with `pd.concat()` and `.merge()` 4. Understand how `pandas` stores data types and missing values, and how types change without warning. 5. Rename and drop columns, and write a multi-step cleaning pipeline that is readable. ## Packages and data ::: {#a65e0d99 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import os import glob import numpy as np import pandas as pd from io import StringIO ``` ::: The [Palmer penguins](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/articles/intro.html) data record body measurements for 344 penguins of three species (Adelie, Chinstrap, Gentoo) living on three islands in Antarctica. ::: {#fb9f40c8 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins = pd.read_csv(os.path.join("assets", "penguins.csv")) penguins.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g sex year
0 Adelie Torgersen 39.1 18.7 181.0 3750.0 male 2007
1 Adelie Torgersen 39.5 17.4 186.0 3800.0 female 2007
2 Adelie Torgersen 40.3 18.0 195.0 3250.0 female 2007
3 Adelie Torgersen NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN 2007
4 Adelie Torgersen 36.7 19.3 193.0 3450.0 female 2007
``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning} ## Don't be misled by the first or last entries Look at `species` in the first five rows. Is that what the whole table looks like? ::: {#2b987a0d .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins["species"].value_counts() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` species Adelie 152 Gentoo 124 Chinstrap 68 Name: count, dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: The file is stored species by species, so the first rows are all Adelie penguins. Never judge a table by its first few rows. `pandas` makes it easy to inspect a random sample: ::: {#bdfb8cc0 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins.sample(5, random_state=1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g sex year
306 Chinstrap Dream 40.9 16.6 187.0 3200.0 female 2008
341 Chinstrap Dream 49.6 18.2 193.0 3775.0 male 2009
291 Chinstrap Dream 50.5 19.6 201.0 4050.0 male 2007
102 Adelie Biscoe 37.7 16.0 183.0 3075.0 female 2009
289 Chinstrap Dream 52.0 18.1 201.0 4050.0 male 2007
``` ::: ::: `random_state` makes the "random" draw repeatable, so you and a classmate see the same rows. ::: ## Indexing and subsetting Every `DataFrame` has **row labels** (the index) and **column labels**. There are two ways to point at a piece of the table: | By | Tool | Meaning | |---------|---------|------------------------------------------| | label | `.loc` | "the row *named* ..., the column *named* ..." | | position| `.iloc` | "the *3rd* row, the *2nd* column" (counting from 0) | To see the difference, we need row labels that are not just the numbers 0, 1, 2, ... Here are six penguins, one for every 60th row, with names for row labels: ::: {#fa4ac96b .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} tmp = penguins[::60].copy() tmp.index = ["Albert", "Beatrix", "Carlos", "Daniela", "Elizabeth", "Fatima"] tmp ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g sex year
Albert Adelie Torgersen 39.1 18.7 181.0 3750.0 male 2007
Beatrix Adelie Biscoe 35.7 16.9 185.0 3150.0 female 2008
Carlos Adelie Torgersen 36.2 17.2 187.0 3150.0 female 2009
Daniela Gentoo Biscoe 48.2 14.3 210.0 4600.0 female 2007
Elizabeth Gentoo Biscoe 47.5 14.0 212.0 4875.0 female 2009
Fatima Chinstrap Dream 46.7 17.9 195.0 3300.0 female 2007
``` ::: ::: ### Rows ::: {#256d90f8 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} tmp.loc["Carlos"] # by label ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` species Adelie island Torgersen bill_length_mm 36.2 bill_depth_mm 17.2 flipper_length_mm 187.0 body_mass_g 3150.0 sex female year 2009 Name: Carlos, dtype: object ``` ::: ::: ::: {#96c352f4 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} tmp.iloc[2] # by position: the same row ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` species Adelie island Torgersen bill_length_mm 36.2 bill_depth_mm 17.2 flipper_length_mm 187.0 body_mass_g 3150.0 sex female year 2009 Name: Carlos, dtype: object ``` ::: ::: Both return one row as a `Series`. Slices work with both, but there is a trap: ::: {#1b11a925 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} tmp.loc["Beatrix":"Daniela"] # label slice: includes BOTH ends ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}
species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g sex year
Beatrix Adelie Biscoe 35.7 16.9 185.0 3150.0 female 2008
Carlos Adelie Torgersen 36.2 17.2 187.0 3150.0 female 2009
Daniela Gentoo Biscoe 48.2 14.3 210.0 4600.0 female 2007
``` ::: ::: ::: {#99173d1a .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} tmp.iloc[1:4] # position slice: stops BEFORE the end, like a Python list ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}
species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g sex year
Beatrix Adelie Biscoe 35.7 16.9 185.0 3150.0 female 2008
Carlos Adelie Torgersen 36.2 17.2 187.0 3150.0 female 2009
Daniela Gentoo Biscoe 48.2 14.3 210.0 4600.0 female 2007
``` ::: ::: These give the same three rows, because `.loc` slices include the last label and `.iloc` slices exclude the last position. ### Rows and columns together Give `.loc` or `.iloc` two inputs: `[rows, columns]`. A bare `:` means "all". ::: {#015ca3c8 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} tmp.loc[:, ["species", "body_mass_g"]] # all rows, two named columns ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}
species body_mass_g
Albert Adelie 3750.0
Beatrix Adelie 3150.0
Carlos Adelie 3150.0
Daniela Gentoo 4600.0
Elizabeth Gentoo 4875.0
Fatima Chinstrap 3300.0
``` ::: ::: ::: {#e9adae47 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} tmp.iloc[1:3, 0:3] # rows 1-2, columns 0-2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ```{=html}
species island bill_length_mm
Beatrix Adelie Biscoe 35.7
Carlos Adelie Torgersen 36.2
``` ::: ::: ### Filtering with `.loc` A **boolean mask** is a column of `True`/`False` values, one per row. Combine one with a list of columns to say "these rows, those columns": ::: {#5a4c19ab .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} tmp.loc[tmp["body_mass_g"] > 4000, ["species", "body_mass_g", "sex"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ```{=html}
species body_mass_g sex
Daniela Gentoo 4600.0 female
Elizabeth Gentoo 4875.0 female
``` ::: ::: This is the version to prefer: the rows and columns are chosen in one step.Square brackets (`df[...]`) also work for quick selections: | Syntax | Returns | |-------------------------|----------------------------------| | `df["a"]` | one column, as a `Series` | | `df[["a", "b"]]` | several columns, as a `DataFrame`| | `df[5:10]` | rows 5 to 9 (a slice by position)| | `df[mask]` | rows where `mask` is `True` | ### Changing values `.loc` can also be used on the left of an `=` to change values in place: ::: {#c3d06c8f .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} tmp.loc["Daniela", "body_mass_g"] = 5000.0 # one cell tmp.loc[tmp["species"] == "Gentoo", "island"] = "Biscoe (check)" # all rows matching a condition tmp ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ```{=html}
species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g sex year
Albert Adelie Torgersen 39.1 18.7 181.0 3750.0 male 2007
Beatrix Adelie Biscoe 35.7 16.9 185.0 3150.0 female 2008
Carlos Adelie Torgersen 36.2 17.2 187.0 3150.0 female 2009
Daniela Gentoo Biscoe (check) 48.2 14.3 210.0 5000.0 female 2007
Elizabeth Gentoo Biscoe (check) 47.5 14.0 212.0 4875.0 female 2009
Fatima Chinstrap Dream 46.7 17.9 195.0 3300.0 female 2007
``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning} ## Chained assignment does nothing Selecting first and assigning second is a common mistake: ::: {#a8ab1749 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} tmp[tmp["species"] == "Gentoo"]["body_mass_g"] = 0 tmp[["species", "body_mass_g"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` /var/folders/1t/yswxk6js3599jsmty8k22m980000gn/T/ipykernel_32916/160912952.py:1: ChainedAssignmentError: A value is being set on a copy of a DataFrame or Series through chained assignment. Such chained assignment never works to update the original DataFrame or Series, because the intermediate object on which we are setting values always behaves as a copy (due to Copy-on-Write). Try using '.loc[row_indexer, col_indexer] = value' instead, to perform the assignment in a single step. See the documentation for a more detailed explanation: https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/user_guide/copy_on_write.html#chained-assignment tmp[tmp["species"] == "Gentoo"]["body_mass_g"] = 0 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ```{=html}
species body_mass_g
Albert Adelie 3750.0
Beatrix Adelie 3150.0
Carlos Adelie 3150.0
Daniela Gentoo 5000.0
Elizabeth Gentoo 4875.0
Fatima Chinstrap 3300.0
``` ::: ::: `tmp[mask]` produces a *new* temporary table, so the assignment lands on the temporary copy and is thrown away. `pandas` may warn you, but the values in `tmp` are unchanged. Always assign in a single `.loc[rows, column] = value` step. ::: ## Reading files `pd.read_csv()` has dozens of options. The following sections catalogue the options you are most likely to use in practice. ### Partial loading ::: {#723062c9 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} path = os.path.join("assets", "penguins.csv") # peek at the first few rows without loading everything pd.read_csv(path, nrows=5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ```{=html}
species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g sex year
0 Adelie Torgersen 39.1 18.7 181.0 3750.0 male 2007
1 Adelie Torgersen 39.5 17.4 186.0 3800.0 female 2007
2 Adelie Torgersen 40.3 18.0 195.0 3250.0 female 2007
3 Adelie Torgersen NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN 2007
4 Adelie Torgersen 36.7 19.3 193.0 3450.0 female 2007
``` ::: ::: ::: {#c04962fb .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} # only some columns, chosen by name (or by position, e.g. [0, 1, 6]) pd.read_csv(path, usecols=["species", "island", "sex"]).head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ```{=html}
species island sex
0 Adelie Torgersen male
1 Adelie Torgersen female
2 Adelie Torgersen female
3 Adelie Torgersen NaN
4 Adelie Torgersen female
``` ::: ::: ::: {#82678073 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} # skip data rows 1-299 (row 0 is the header line, which we keep) pd.read_csv(path, skiprows=range(1, 300)).head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ```{=html}
species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g sex year
0 Chinstrap Dream 50.6 19.4 193 3800 male 2007
1 Chinstrap Dream 46.7 17.9 195 3300 female 2007
2 Chinstrap Dream 52.0 19.0 197 4150 male 2007
3 Chinstrap Dream 50.5 18.4 200 3400 female 2008
4 Chinstrap Dream 49.5 19.0 200 3800 male 2008
``` ::: ::: ### Specifying structure `pandas` guesses the type of each column. The guess is likely to be wrong whenever a file uses its own conventions. Here is a small file that uses `-999` and the word `missing` for unknown values, and has a date column: ::: {#fba7a387 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} raw = """id,date,amount,region 001,2025-03-01,19.99,West 002,2025-03-02,-999,East 003,2025-03-05,24.50,missing 004,2025-03-09,7.25,West""" naive = pd.read_csv(StringIO(raw)) naive ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=18} ```{=html}
id date amount region
0 1 2025-03-01 19.99 West
1 2 2025-03-02 -999.00 East
2 3 2025-03-05 24.50 missing
3 4 2025-03-09 7.25 West
``` ::: ::: ::: {#c20c4a7d .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} naive.dtypes ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=19} ``` id int64 date str amount float64 region str dtype: object ``` ::: ::: Three things went wrong: 1. `id` lost its leading zeros, 2. `date` is just text, and 3. `-999` is being treated as a real amount (it would drag an average down). We fix each with a reader option: ::: {#a5900df7 .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} better = pd.read_csv( StringIO(raw), na_values=["-999", "missing"], # extra strings that mean "missing" parse_dates=["date"], # convert to real dates dtype={"id": str}, # keep as text, preserving "001" ) better ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=20} ```{=html}
id date amount region
0 001 2025-03-01 19.99 West
1 002 2025-03-02 NaN East
2 003 2025-03-05 24.50 NaN
3 004 2025-03-09 7.25 West
``` ::: ::: ::: {#a97a4337 .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} better.dtypes ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=21} ``` id str date datetime64[us] amount float64 region str dtype: object ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip} `pandas` already treats empty cells and the text `NA` as missing. You only need `na_values` for *additional* codes like `-999`. Familiarize yourself with missing value conventions of different systems. ::: ## Writing files Methods named `.to_*()` export a table. `.to_csv()` is the most common. ::: {#eef50ade .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} os.makedirs("output", exist_ok=True) # create a folder for our results for species, group in penguins.groupby("species"): filepath = os.path.join("output", f"penguins_{species}.csv") group.to_csv(filepath, index=False) print("saved", filepath, group.shape) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` saved output/penguins_Adelie.csv (152, 8) saved output/penguins_Chinstrap.csv (68, 8) saved output/penguins_Gentoo.csv (124, 8) ``` ::: ::: `index=False` avoids writing the row labels as an extra column. When the row labels are just 0, 1, 2, ..., that is what you want. ::: {.callout-warning} ## When the index holds information If the index carries real information, such as a summary table whose rows are labeled by species, then `index=False` throws it away and you cannot tell which row is which. Use `.reset_index()` first to turn the labels into an ordinary column. ::: Common reasons to export: - saving a cleaned copy for later, sharing a summary table, and - **saving intermediate results in a long pipeline** so you do not have to rerun everything. ### Combining many files Data often arrive in pieces: one file per month, per region, or per species. `glob` finds the files matching a pattern; `pd.concat()` stacks the tables. ::: {#04a8a5b2 .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} files = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join("output", "penguins_*.csv"))) files ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=23} ``` ['output/penguins_Adelie.csv', 'output/penguins_Chinstrap.csv', 'output/penguins_Gentoo.csv'] ``` ::: ::: ::: {#1f69de08 .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} combined = pd.concat( [pd.read_csv(f).assign(source_file = os.path.basename(f)) for f in files], ignore_index = True, ) print(combined.shape) combined["source_file"].value_counts() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (344, 9) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=24} ``` source_file penguins_Adelie.csv 152 penguins_Gentoo.csv 124 penguins_Chinstrap.csv 68 Name: count, dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: - `sorted()` makes the file order the same on every computer. - `.assign(source_file=...)` records which file each row came from. This costs nothing now and is very helpful when you later find a strange value. - `ignore_index=True` renumbers the rows 0, 1, 2, ... instead of repeating each file's own numbering. ## Combining tables | Tool | What it does | Use when | |---------------|----------------------------------------------------------|----------| | `pd.concat()` | **Stacks** tables on top of each other | the tables have the *same columns* (e.g. one file per month) | | `.merge()` | **Matches** rows using a shared column (a *key*), adding columns | one table describes things in another (e.g. a lookup table) | ### Merging Suppose a colleague gives us a small table of extra information about each island. (This table is made up, purely for illustration.) ::: {#3d67e4bc .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} island_info = pd.DataFrame({ "island": ["Biscoe", "Dream"], "survey_team": ["Team A", "Team B"], }) island_info ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=25} ```{=html}
island survey_team
0 Biscoe Team A
1 Dream Team B
``` ::: ::: Notice that Torgersen is missing from the lookup table. Let us merge it onto the penguins: ::: {#16e800fd .cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} left = penguins.merge(island_info, on = "island", how = "left" ) left.loc[left["island"] == "Torgersen", ["species", "island", "survey_team"]].head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=26} ```{=html}
species island survey_team
0 Adelie Torgersen NaN
1 Adelie Torgersen NaN
2 Adelie Torgersen NaN
``` ::: ::: Notice this table has shape (344, 9). ::: {#e98aad00 .cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} inner = penguins.merge(island_info, on = "island", how = "inner" ) inner.loc[inner["island"] == "Torgersen", ["species", "island", "survey_team"]].head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=27} ```{=html}
species island survey_team
``` ::: ::: Notice this table has shape (292, 9). - `how = "left"` keeps **every row of the left table** (`penguins`) and fills in `NaN` where the lookup has no match. - `how = "inner"` keeps **only rows that match in both tables**, so the Torgersen penguins quietly disappeared. Neither is wrong, but you must know which one you chose. A good habit after *every* merge is to compare the number of rows before and after, and count the unmatched rows. - In the `left` merge example, there were 344 rows before the merge and 344 rows after the merge. - There are 52 penguins missing `island` information. ### Duplicate keys What if the lookup table has the same key twice? ::: {#ade472bf .cell execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code} island_info_dup = pd.concat([island_info, island_info.iloc[[0]]], ignore_index=True) island_info_dup ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=28} ```{=html}
island survey_team
0 Biscoe Team A
1 Dream Team B
2 Biscoe Team A
``` ::: ::: ::: {#47b76432 .cell execution_count=29} ``` {.python .cell-code} dup = penguins.merge(island_info_dup, on = "island", how = "left" ) print(len(penguins), "->", len(dup)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 344 -> 512 ``` ::: ::: Every Biscoe penguin now appears twice, so any total or count you compute afterwards is wrong. You can ask `pandas` to check the relationship and stop with an error if it is violated: ::: {#806e21f5 .cell execution_count=30} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins.merge(island_info_dup, on = "island", how = "left", validate = "many_to_one" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: `"many_to_one"` says: many rows on the left may match one row on the right, but not the reverse. ## Data types ::: {#f8ea6305 .cell execution_count=31} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins.dtypes ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=31} ``` species str island str bill_length_mm float64 bill_depth_mm float64 flipper_length_mm float64 body_mass_g float64 sex str year int64 dtype: object ``` ::: ::: - `float64`: numbers with decimals (and missing values, stored as `NaN`). - `int64`: whole numbers. **These cannot hold a missing value.** - `str`: text. A missing text value is also `NaN`. ### Silent casting An integer column that gains a missing value silently converts data to `float`: ::: {#5492e95f .cell execution_count=32} ``` {.python .cell-code} years = penguins["year"].head(5).copy() print(years.dtype) years[0] = None print(years.dtype) years ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` int64 float64 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=32} ``` 0 NaN 1 2007.0 2 2007.0 3 2007.0 4 2007.0 Name: year, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: If you need whole numbers *and* missing values, ask for the nullable integer type, written with a capital `I`: ::: {#502af75d .cell execution_count=33} ``` {.python .cell-code} years.astype("Int64") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=33} ``` 0 1 2007 2 2007 3 2007 4 2007 Name: year, dtype: Int64 ``` ::: ::: Here the missing value is shown as ``. ### Converting types `.astype()` converts a column. Here are two conversion you are likely to use in practice: ::: {#5454fb56 .cell execution_count=34} ``` {.python .cell-code} # whole numbers with possible missing values penguins["year"].astype("Int64").dtype ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=34} ``` Int64Dtype() ``` ::: ::: ::: {#76d06db8 .cell execution_count=35} ``` {.python .cell-code} # a column with a fixed set of labels can be stored as a category penguins["species"].astype("category").dtype ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=35} ``` CategoricalDtype(categories=['Adelie', 'Chinstrap', 'Gentoo'], ordered=False, categories_dtype=str) ``` ::: ::: A `category` can also have a **meaningful order**. Plain text sorts alphabetically, which is rarely the order you want for **ordinal data** (such as ratings or sizes): ::: {#fc9cb57d .cell execution_count=36} ``` {.python .cell-code} sizes = pd.Series( ["medium", "small", "large", "small", "large", "medium"] ) print(sizes.sort_values().tolist()) # alphabetical size_type = pd.CategoricalDtype( ["small", "medium", "large"], ordered=True ) sizes_cat = sizes.astype(size_type) print(sizes_cat.sort_values().tolist()) # in the order we specified ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ['large', 'large', 'medium', 'medium', 'small', 'small'] ['small', 'small', 'medium', 'medium', 'large', 'large'] ``` ::: ::: ### Statistics and missing values Most summary methods skip missing values by default, which is convenient but easy to forget. ::: {#ccf96922 .cell execution_count=37} ``` {.python .cell-code} cols = penguins[["bill_length_mm", "body_mass_g"]] cols.mean() # skipna = True: missing values ignored ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=37} ``` bill_length_mm 43.921930 body_mass_g 4201.754386 dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#62ce1aca .cell execution_count=38} ``` {.python .cell-code} cols.mean(skipna = False) # any missing value makes the answer NaN ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=38} ``` bill_length_mm NaN body_mass_g NaN dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: Double-check the sample size used in calculating summary statistics: ::: {#dd3107f5 .cell execution_count=39} ``` {.python .cell-code} cols.count() # how many values each mean is based on ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=39} ``` bill_length_mm 342 body_mass_g 342 dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: The `axis` option says which direction to compute in. - The default `axis=0` collapses the rows (one answer per column). - `axis=1` collapses the columns (one answer per row). ::: {#15279aa7 .cell execution_count=40} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins[["bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm"]].mean(axis=1).head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=40} ``` 0 28.90 1 28.45 2 29.15 3 NaN 4 28.00 dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: :::: callout-warning Remember that averaging across columns like this only makes sense if the data have the same units. :::: ## Changing the shape of a table ### Renaming and dropping Most methods return a **new** table and leave the original alone. Save the result to a variable to keep it. ::: {#39946dad .cell execution_count=41} ``` {.python .cell-code} renamed = penguins.rename( columns={"body_mass_g": "mass_g", "island": "home"} ) renamed.columns.tolist() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=41} ``` ['species', 'home', 'bill_length_mm', 'bill_depth_mm', 'flipper_length_mm', 'mass_g', 'sex', 'year'] ``` ::: ::: ::: {#3b593cb7 .cell execution_count=42} ``` {.python .cell-code} slim = penguins.drop(columns=["year", "sex"]) # drop columns by name slim.columns.tolist() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=42} ``` ['species', 'island', 'bill_length_mm', 'bill_depth_mm', 'flipper_length_mm', 'body_mass_g'] ``` ::: ::: ::: {#b4624786 .cell execution_count=43} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins.columns.tolist() # the original is unchanged ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=43} ``` ['species', 'island', 'bill_length_mm', 'bill_depth_mm', 'flipper_length_mm', 'body_mass_g', 'sex', 'year'] ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## Why we avoid `inplace = True` Many methods accept `inplace = True`, which modifies the table you called it on. It is easy to run twice by accident, it cannot be chained, and the `pandas` developers recommend against it. Prefer reassignment; for example `df = df.method(...)`. This style makes it easy to spot where a table changes in your code. ::: ### Adding rows Rows are best added by building them first and stacking them once with `concat`: ::: {#f6834e9e .cell execution_count=44} ``` {.python .cell-code} new_rows = pd.DataFrame([ { "species": "Gentoo", "island": "Torgersen", "bill_length_mm": 35.0, "bill_depth_mm": 20.0, "flipper_length_mm": 180.0, "body_mass_g": 3500.0, "sex": "female", "year": 2025 }, ]) extended = pd.concat([penguins, new_rows], ignore_index = True) extended.tail(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=44} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: You might see `df.loc[len(df)] = row` in online examples. Unfortunately, that style silently copies the whole table every time and is slow in a loop. ## Method chaining A **pipeline** applies several operations in a row, each acting on the result of the previous one. Wrap the whole expression in parentheses so you can put one step on each line: ::: {#885ac0ef .cell execution_count=45} ``` {.python .cell-code} ( penguins .dropna(subset = ["body_mass_g"]) .assign(mass_kg = lambda d: d["body_mass_g"] / 1000) .query("mass_kg > 5") .sort_values("mass_kg", ascending = False) .loc[:, ["species", "island", "sex", "mass_kg"]] .head() ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=45} ```{=html}
species island sex mass_kg
169 Gentoo Biscoe male 6.30
185 Gentoo Biscoe male 6.05
269 Gentoo Biscoe male 6.00
229 Gentoo Biscoe male 6.00
263 Gentoo Biscoe male 5.95
``` ::: ::: - `.assign(name = ...)` creates a new column. - The `lambda d: ...` syntax defines an anonymous function. Here `d` stands for "the table as it is at this point in the pipeline". - Each line does one thing, so the code reads like a recipe, and you can comment out a line to see what it did. - If a chain becomes long or confusing, break it into smaller steps with names for the intermediate tables. ## Summary | Task | Code | |-------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------| | Row by label / position | `df.loc[label]`, `df.iloc[k]` | | Rows and columns together | `df.loc[mask, ["a", "b"]]`, `df.iloc[1:3, 0:3]`| | Change values | `df.loc[mask, "col"] = value` | | Read part of a file | `nrows=`, `usecols=`, `skiprows=` | | Declare missing codes, dates, types | `na_values=`, `parse_dates=`, `dtype=` | | Write a file | `df.to_csv(path, index=False)` | | Stack tables / many files | `pd.concat([...], ignore_index=True)` | | Match tables on a key | `left.merge(right, on="key", how="left")` | | Check a merge | compare row counts; `validate="many_to_one"` | | Missing-friendly integers | `.astype("Int64")` | | Rename / drop columns | `df.rename(columns={...})`, `df.drop(columns=[...])` | | Pipeline | `(df.step1().step2().step3())` | ## Exercises Use the `penguins` table loaded at the top. ### Exercise 1: Reading 1.
